title: Floating-point numbers, representation and manipulation
overview: Binary floating-point representation stores a real number using a mantissa and an exponent. For Cambridge 9618 both fields are interpreted using two's complement. You must convert values, normalise them, and explain precision, range, rounding, overflow and underflow.
syllabusPoints: Interpret mantissa and exponent fields in binary floating-point values.
Convert between floating-point binary and denary.
Explain how mantissa/exponent bit allocation affects precision and range and why rounding errors occur.

definitions.definition: The signed significant part of a floating-point number; more mantissa bits give greater precision.
The signed power of two controlling the position of the binary point; more exponent bits give greater range.
Rewriting a floating-point number in a standard form that uses the mantissa bits efficiently.
The difference caused when an exact value cannot be represented with the available bits.
A value whose magnitude is too large for the available exponent range.
A non-zero value too close to zero to be represented usefully with the available format.

sections.title: Interpreting the format
content: Think of the value as mantissa multiplied by 2 raised to the exponent. Decode the exponent carefully, then move the binary point by that signed power.

sections.title: Precision versus range
content: More mantissa bits provide more significant binary digits, so nearby values can be distinguished more accurately. More exponent bits allow larger positive and negative exponents, expanding the representable range. With a fixed word length, increasing one usually reduces the other.

sections.title: Normalisation
content: Normalisation avoids wasting mantissa bits on redundant sign bits. In two's-complement fractional form, a positive normalised mantissa begins with different leading sign/data bits (typically 01...) and a negative one typically begins 10....

sections.title: Approximation and rounding
content: Many denary fractions recur forever in binary, so finite storage keeps an approximation. Repeated arithmetic can accumulate small errors; this is why equality comparisons on calculated real values can be unreliable.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.content: 0.1 in denary has a recurring binary fractional representation.

sections.title: Overflow and underflow
content: Overflow is a range failure at very large magnitude; underflow occurs near zero when the format cannot keep a meaningful non-zero representation. Increasing exponent bits changes range, not the significant precision of the mantissa.

examTips: Write binary place values before converting to avoid moving the point in the wrong direction.
State the trade-off explicitly: mantissa -> precision; exponent -> range.
Do not forget that the exponent is signed.
commonMistakes: Saying exponent bits directly increase precision.
Assuming every denary fraction has an exact finite binary representation.
